How do you go about finding news that isn't click bait? How do you find the news you want to read?
I read lots of sources some right leaning some left-leaning. I like having both sides of a story line, because, the truth lies somewhere in the middle

First thing after I get up, while grabbing my morning vape, I cruise through the headlines on the Guardian's app. This gives me a spread of both world and US news, plus tech, science, and a couple custom tags. Celebrity and sports are removed from my main page there. Not always anything interesting, which is something I note in itself.

There's usually some alerts in Twitter to take a look at. If there's anything going on in the realm of my interests I'll likely have a notification to peak at. Only takes a few minutes to clear those and take a look at the "while you were gone" section. Read some articles, get a feel for the headlines, finish my tea and grab a bowl of cereal.

While I munch on my cinnamon toast crunch I crack open the laptop and refresh the RSS tab in Thunderbird. The little popping noise as the unread counts start climbing always gives me a smile. Open the news tab and see what's new at The Intercept and a few local sources. Skim some summaries, open a few full articles into the browser, then jump over to webcomics. Usually 10 or so there to make me smile after the frowns and sneers generated in the previous folder.

Move onto the tech feeds. Masnick sassing the FBI again? Schnier post anything informative? Any chatter about things I might want later? Usually! Open these things into Firefox, hit sync, and get dressed.

Through the day I can open Firefox on my phone and grab whatever synced tabs I have time to read during slack time at work. Twitter or Guardian will pop up any breaking news, plus if multiple people I follow are talking about the same thing I get a notice. That can be informative.

http://digg.com/

Most world events or big things that are happening on the internet show up on there. Picture to go along with each article, a small summary so I can tell if I want to spend time reading the whole thing, and enough variety that I can find something I actually want to read.

Also there's a limited amount of new articles per day, so I'm not scrolling thru endless links for hours every day.
I used Google News for a while, but I couldn't figure out how to get it to remove Top Stories, and it is in fact Top Stories that I most want to get rid of.

I generally avoid the news, as it is usually depressing, and I'll find out about anything really big from other sources. So I confine most of my news reading to hyperlocal news about what new bar has opened, etc., and news related directly to my profession.

Aside from Voat? I am into hard news, and I study economics in college so I have to be a news junkie to stay on top of things.

When I wake up in the morning I pull up the DoggCatcher RSS client on my cell phone. I use it to listen to 5 minute news updates from NPR and CBC while I brush my teeth and have breakfast. I usually listen to most of the 30 minute BBC news update. All 3 of these podcasts are updated hourly.

I have a folder of good news sources on my bookmarks bar. The ones I hit regularly are Bloomberg, NYT, Google News, Vice and Reuters. I also subscribe to the Economist and I usually listen to their weekly edition on my cell phone using their app when I'm playing video games. I always listen to NPR while I drive. I watch the Philip DeFranco show on YouTube a few times a week.

Most of the stuff published in the NYT or Washington Post is softened editorialized garbage that I have no patience for any more. Every now and then they post something good and when they do it shows up on Google News. I put them and a lot of other major American news outlets in the same category as my friends blogs, because they don't really investigate as well as other outlets. Bloomberg is constantly in lawsuits over their sunshine law requests. I can't remember the last time the Washington Post or the NYT or CNN tangled with the government like that (well, not since Wikileaks, but in the end the NYT did the American government's bidding in that situation so fuck them).

Cable news is complete garbage. Years ago I used to watch CNN obsessively, then HLN, then nothing. I cut the chord because they aren't serious about covering current events. The only time I watch TV is for the Daily Show, sometimes. When it turns into Stewart just making fun of people I don't recognize or care about on Fox news then it's time to turn the TV off and do something productive. I mean, we get it, Fox news is bad... the gag is too old to entertain me now.

NPR was where I started losing interest in news. They seem to be stuck in the Sixties, and they only talk about certain stories and always with the same perspective. I still occasionally pick up their hourly, but it almost never says anything I haven't already heard elsewhere and in greater depth.

I have the CBC smartphone app, but they seem to carry mostly AP plus Canadian stories, and I am really trying to get away from most of what the AP covers. And I hasten to add, I don't care about local stories in Canada almost all the time.

NPR hourlies aren't bad for just getting the basic idea of what is in the current news cycle quickly, which is really all I want in exchange for my 5 minutes. I don't care much about analysis or editorial content. I'll analyze things myself anyway.
